recognized: Think about a time you needed to read a letter, hear instructions, or remember an appointment. You already know how to judge whether those everyday tools help you. We will apply that judgment to a computer. Choose one task that matters to you. Reading a library page, joining a practice call, or keeping a household reminder. You do not need to know every setting. Our goal is to choose one useful change, observe the result, and know how to undo it. Keep a scrap of paper nearby to record the original setting. That makes experimenting safer, especially on a shared lab computer.

Imagine the library page is difficult to read, but the computer's other menus look comfortable. Start with the browser's Zoom control, because the problem is inside that page. Open the browser menu, find Zoom, and increase it one step. On many Windows browsers, Control and Plus also zooms in. Control and Zero returns to the default. Watch the page get larger, then check the important part. Can you still find the search field, read the instructions, and reach the button, larger is useful only if the task still works. Pause the video, try one Zoom step on a practice page, and restore it before continuing.

Now, suppose the browser tabs and the rest of the desktop are also hard to see. PageZoom will not solve every part of that problem. System text size changes text in supported areas. Display scaling changes the size of text, apps, and other interface elements more broadly. The exact controls depend on your computer. Ask the instructor before changing a shared workstation's system settings. This is like choosing between a magnifying glass for one page and a more comfortable arrangement for the whole desk. Which would you try first if only one website is too small? Browser zoom, because it matches the scope of the problem.

Picture a radio connected to headphones. Turning up the radio does not make the room speaker play if the sound is still going to the headphones. A computer can work the same way. First, check whether the sound is muted. Then, inspect the selected output device, speakers, a monitor, or a headset. Choose the device you intend to hear, begin at a comfortable volume, and play a short test. If that test works but a meeting does not, check the meeting app's own audio choice next. Change one setting at a time. This gives you evidence about what fixed the problem instead of leaving you with several unexplained changes.

A slow computer and a full computer are not exactly the same problem. The processor carries out instructions. Working memory holds information in active use, while storage keeps saved files. Think of a workbench and a filing cabinet. A crowded workbench and a full cabinet require different responses. Closing an unused app may reduce active workload. It does not create a reliable backup of your files. For connections, identify the job before choosing the cable. A display connection carries a picture, a network connection carries data, and a USB connection may carry data or power depending on the equipment. Match the labels and ask before forcing an unfamiliar connector.

Suppose you want one page of directions for a community event. Open Print Preview before sending anything to the printer. Check the destination first. A physical printer and Save as PDF produce different results. Next, inspect the page count, orientation, and selected range. A web page may create extra pages containing menus or blank space. Choose one useful page, look for clipped text, and print a single test copy. Only then print more. If the printer does not respond, check its status or queue and ask for help rather than repeatedly pressing print. Repeated requests can arrive later as an unexpected stack of duplicates.

A paper calendar works because a short note connects a time to an action. A digital entry needs the same meaning. In our fictional example, create library practice from 2 to 3 in the afternoon with room A as the location. Check the correct day, start time, end time, and time zone when one is shown. Add a reminder early enough to help you prepare. Day view helps inspect the details. Week view helps notice conflicts. month view gives a wider overview. Change the view and find the same appointment again. Saving an entry is only the first step. Reopening it confirms that the details survived.

Your partner needs to choose a meeting time but does not need every detail of your calendar. Free or busy sharing can communicate that a time is occupied without exposing its title or location. Compare the two views. Your calendar contains library practice and room A. Your partner sees only busy. Before sharing, read the actual services options because not every calendar offers identical controls. Ask who needs access, what they need to know, and for how long. Pause and decide. Should someone arranging a study session automatically receive private appointment details? No. Start with availability, then share more only when the task calls for it.

Reminders, saved browser preferences, and cloud services can save effort, but automation still needs a check. A cloud service runs on another computer and often connects your work to an account. Confirm which account is active before saving or sharing. After setting a reminder, check that notifications are allowed and that the reminder time is sensible. If you need help, use instructions from the software's official support site and match them to your version. A menu from an older version may look different. Describe the task and what happened. I selected the headset, but the test sound still plays through the monitor. That is useful evidence for a helper.

Now pause and choose one improvement that matters to your own routine. Make a practice page comfortable to read, route a test sound to the intended device, or create a fictional calendar entry. Tell a partner what you expected before you act, then show the result and explain how to undo the change. If the result is different from your prediction, return to the original setting and try a smaller step. Before leaving, save your practice work, restore shared settings, and sign out of any demonstration account as directed. The skill is not memorizing every menu. It is choosing a change, checking evidence, and repeating a routine you can use elsewhere.

Imagine a neighbor asks where they can get help using a computer. You may already have a familiar library, community center, or veterans organization in mind. Use that experience as a starting point, then verify what is available now. Today's search tools answer in full sentences, so our first skill is asking well, and our second is checking what the answer says. Our task is to find a suitable public service, record enough evidence to revisit it, and and organize a fictional handout without exposing private information. You can use a different local service that matters to you. The names and details in this demonstration are examples, not a claim about any particular organization. A useful search ends with a supported decision, not just an answer that sounds confident

search tools now answer in sentences. Google may show an AI overview above the results, and AI mode lets you keep asking follow -up questions. Both work best when you ask the way you would ask a librarian. Say what you need, where you are, and what matters to you. Where can I get free computer help near Beckley, West Virginia in the evening? Is far more useful than computer help? If the first answer is too broad, ask a follow -up such as, which of these are open on Saturdays? Pause and write a question for your chosen community task. Include the service, the place, and one detail that matters to you. Then, ask one follow -up.

An AI answer is a quick summary written from many pages. It can sound sure and still be wrong, out of date, or about a different town. So treat it as a lead, not a source. Look for the links beside or beneath it and open the organization's own page. Ask who published it, when it was updated, and whether it answers your question. If the summary and the page disagree, trust the responsible organization and confirm hours by phone before you travel. Never type private details into a question, such as a social security number, a bank number, or medical information. Pause, open one source from your answer, and find one detail it confirms and one it does not.

Suppose you find a useful service today and need it again next month. A note saying, good website, will not be enough. Record the organization, the page title, the web address, the date you checked it, and the particular fact you plan to use. If an AI answer led you to the page, record the page it pointed to, not the summary. A bookmark helps you return, but it does not freeze the page or prove that the information remains current. In your handout, distinguish a checked fact from your own interpretation. If the page does not answer a question, write, needs confirmation, rather than filling the gap with a guess. This is the digital equivalent of writing the source beside a number in a household notebook.

An online form is a structured request. Read its purpose and required fields before typing. In our course practice form, choose the kind of computer help needed and a fictional contact preference. Review the entries before selecting the final button. On a real service, ask whether a sensitive detail is necessary for the task, and verify the site before entering it. Our practice does not send a real request. That distinction matters. Seeing a confirmation message in a simulator proves that you completed the exercise. Not that an organization received anything. Pause, complete the fictional form, and explain what you deliberately left out and why.

Think of a folder as a labeled place to put related work. Create a practice folder for the community resource task and use a descriptive file name, such as library -help -draft. A file saved on this computer may not appear on another computer. A cloud file belongs to a service and an account, and a synced folder may keep copies in more than one place. Before moving to another device, check the account and the saving or syncing status. Re -open the file from the intended location. That simple test catches a common mistake, editing one copy while later opening an older copy somewhere else.

Our partner should suggest clearer wording without rewriting the handout directly. Viewer access usually allows reading. Commenter access, when supported, allows suggestions through comments. Editor access permits changes to the content. Choose the smallest role that fits the task, inspect the recipient carefully, and have the partner verify that the file opens with the expected controls. A link that works for you may still fail for someone else. Also distinguish read -only from encryption. Read -only limits editing. It does not necessarily prevent someone from reading or copying the information. Pause and choose a role for someone who only needs to read the finished handout. Viewer is the appropriate starting point.

Sync is convenient because a change can travel between a device and an online service. The same convenience can carry a deletion. Watch the practice file disappear from one location and then the other. That is why Sync alone is not a separate backup. A backup provides another recovery copy under an appropriate plan. Version history may preserve earlier content, while a recycle bin may retain a deleted file for a limited time. availability and retention depend on the service. Do not test deletion with your only important file. Use the fictional copy and explain which protection would help if the mistake spread through every synced location.

First, identify the problem. If the whole file is missing after deletion, inspect the appropriate trash or recycle bin. If the file exists but it's wording changed, inspect version history. Preview the earlier version and coordinate with collaborators before restoring it. You do not want to replace useful work someone just added. Compression is a separate tool. A zip file can package several files for transfer and may reduce their size. it is not automatically encryption or a backup plan. After extracting a practice zip, open a file to confirm the contents are usable. Choose the tool that matches the problem rather than trusting a familiar icon.

Pause and build a small resource folder for your chosen community task. Include a source note, a fictional handout, and a clear file name. Tell a partner which fact you verified, why that source is appropriate, and which permission fits the review task. Then explain how you would recover a deleted file and how that differs from restoring earlier wording. If an account or sharing feature is unavailable, demonstrate the decision with the course simulator and label it simulated. For your next independent task, reuse this sequence. Ask a focused question, check the evidence, record a trail, organize the file, and verify access.

Think about a set of instructions that made a new task easy. Most likely they told you the next step and left nothing to guess. Today you will make a small resource pack for a library computer help session. You will write a handout in Word, total a supply list in Excel, and build three slides in PowerPoint. Then you will save the handout as a PDF and check it the way your reader will. Every choice starts with the reader. Who will pick up this handout and what should they do after reading it? Write one sentence that names your reader and their next step. Pause the video now.

Open a blank Word document and type the handout lines from your worksheet. Select the first line, Computer Help at the Library. On the Home tab, choose Heading 1. Then make Who It Helps and Steps into Heading 2. Bold text only changes how a line looks. A heading style tells Word and a screen reader that a new section starts here. To check, open the View tab and turn on the Navigation pane. Your headings appear in a list on the left. Next, select the three steps and choose Numbering. For the link, select words that name where it goes, such as Read the Computer Help Guide. Press Ctrl and K and type the address.

A few keys save a lot of mouse work. Ctrl and C copies what you selected. Ctrl and V pastes it. Ctrl and Z undoes your last change, so a mistake is easy to take back. Now trade seats with the partner. In their handout, open the Review tab, turn on Track Changes, and change one word to make a step clearer. Word shows your edit in color instead of quietly replacing the text. A comment is different. It explains why, and it changes nothing. Back at your own seat, choose Accept or Reject for each change. The owner always makes the final call. Build your handout, then trade seats and track one edit. Pause the video now.

download supplies .csv from your worksheet and open it in Excel. Columns have letters and rows have numbers, so B2 means column B, row 2. The list has paper at $12, folders at 8, and pens at 5. Change the heading in B1 to cost in dollars, so a reader knows what the numbers mean. Click cell B5 just below the costs. Type an equal sign, then sum, then B2 colon B4 in parentheses, and press enter. The equal sign starts a formula, and the colon means every cell from B2 through B4. B5 shows 25. Before you change anything, predict. If paper costs $15, what will the total be? Enter the formula in your own sheet and write your prediction. Pause the video now.

Now test your prediction. Click B2, type 15, and press Enter. The total changes to 28 by itself, because the formula adds the cells, not a number someone typed. If your total state at 25, click B5 and read the formula bar. A typed number, or a range that skips a cell, will not update. When it works, save it the right way. Choose File, then Save As, and pick Excel Workbook as the type. A CSV file keeps the numbers, but drops the formula. Change paper to 15, check the total against your prediction, and save it as an Excel Workbook. Pause the video now.

Slides work best when each one does one job. The first slide names the need. Need computer help? The second shows the steps. The third says where to go. Use the same three steps as your handout so your reader gets one message, not two. Start PowerPoint with a blank presentation and pick one theme on the Design tab so all three slides match. Keep the words few and large. Then step back from your screen. Can you still read every word? If you have to squint, cut words before you shrink the text.

Insert the practice photo on the first slide. Cropping trims the edges you do not need, so the two people in the handout fill the frame. Resizing changes the size of the whole picture. They solve different problems. There is a catch. A crop only hides the edges. They stay in the file until you compress the picture and delete the cropped areas. Next, add alt text, one sentence that says what the photo shows, for someone who cannot see it. PowerPoint may suggest a description. Check it the way you would check an AI answer. Then add the credit line. Make your three slides, then crop, describe, and credit the photo. Pause the video now.

who gets the file decides the format. A neighbor who only reads it gets a PDF, which looks the same on any computer. A partner who will edit it gets the Word document. A tool that needs plain rows of numbers gets a CSV. Before you export, choose Review, then Check Accessibility. It points out missing headings, missing alt text, and links that do not say where they go. Then, choose File, Save As, and set the type to PDF. Saving is not the last step. Open the PDF from your folder and check the headings, the numbered steps, and the link, because that file is what your reader gets. Save your handout as a PDF. Open it from the folder and check it. Pause the video now.

Short how -to videos need editing, too. Trimming cuts unwanted material at the start or the end. Splitting cuts a clip into pieces, so you can remove a section in the middle, such as a long pause. After every cut, play it back. Did you clip the first word of a sentence? Did you cut the step that explains the result? If the clip has captions, check them against the edited sound, because old captions drift out of time. The video editor in Windows needs a Microsoft account, so today you will use a practice page. Open the Mission 3D practice page, trim the start and end, then remove the pause in the middle. Pause the video now.

Before you call your pack finished, use it the way your reader will. Open the PDF and find the next step without hunting for it. Click the link. In the workbook, change one cost and watch the total follow. Read the second slide from across the room. Each check tests one of today's skills—a handout with real structure, a formula that updates, slides with one message, and an export you opened yourself. Fix the first problem you find, then check again. The same routine works for a club notice, a church bulletin, or a household budget. Make it for a reader, test it, and keep the original.

Think of a group task you have helped organize, such as a family gathering or a volunteer day. Confusion usually starts when people assume someone else knows what to do. Today we plan a fictional Saturday computer help session. You wrote the handout, Sam will review it, Pat organizes the session and keeps the shared copy, Alex runs the session on the day, and 20 volunteers need to hear about it. You will send a clear request, improve one shared copy, take part in a meeting, and check an offer before you pay. The goal is not more messages. It is the right person taking the right next step.

Start by choosing how to reach someone. A detailed request that can wait until tomorrow suits an email because the details stay in writing. An urgent problem in this room needs a word in person right now. A shared document suits work that several people change. Then, check which account you are sending from. In a new email, the from line shows it. A personal account and a volunteer group account reach different people and carry different expectations. Choose a channel for each of the two messages on your worksheet, and say why. Pause the video now.

A useful email answers three questions—what should I do, with which file, and by when. A subject such as, Please review the Computer Help handout by Thursday, tell Sam the job before the email is even opened. In the body, greet Sam, name the part to check, say when you need a reply, and close politely. Spell out abbreviations and drop guesses about anyone's age or skill. Then read it as Sam would. Could Sam act without asking you a question? Write the request to Sam, then rewrite the unclear message on your worksheet so anyone could follow it. Pause the video now.

Before you send, read every recipient line. Sam needs to act, so Sam goes in too. Pat should know, so Pat goes in CC. The volunteers do not need a review request, so take them off. The notice to the volunteers is a different email. There, Alex goes in too, Pat in CC, and the 20 volunteers in BCC, so they cannot see one another's addresses. BCC does not stop anyone from forwarding it. If Pat chooses reply all, it goes to you and Alex, never to the BCC names. Use schedule send so an early draft arrives at a sensible hour. Address the volunteer notice on your worksheet. Pause the video now.

Imagine three people editing three copies of the handout and calling each one final. Nobody knows which instructions to follow. Instead, agree on one shared copy and one place to keep it. Pat, the owner, makes the final call. You write, Sam reviews. Give each person only the access the job needs. Sam can comment, and you and Pat can edit. Working at the same time is called synchronous, leaving comments for later is called asynchronous. Neither is better. Pick the one that fits people's schedules and write the decision in the shared copy. With a partner, choose your roles, your shared place, and how you will work. Pause the video now.

Compare to comments. This is confusing gives the writer nothing to act on. In step 2, add where the desk is, room A on the first floor, so first -time visitors can find it. That comment names a place, a change, and a reason. In Word, select the step, choose Review, then new comment, and type it. The writer replies first, then makes the change or explains why not. Resolve the comment only after that reply. A resolved comment is hidden, not deleted. Comment on the work, never on the person. Trade seats, add one useful comment, then reply to and resolve the comment on your own handout. Pause the video now.

Before a meeting, test your headset. In Windows Settings, under Sound, choose the headset as the input and speak during the test. In the meeting, stay muted unless you are speaking and raise your hand when the host asks for it. Turn on captions if they help. A webinar is different. The host controls who can speak, so questions go in the Q &A box or the chat. Ask before you record anyone, especially a group sharing personal stories. If your sound fails partway through, use the backup the host gave you, such as the chat or the shared notes.

A community page can point you to a pantry, a class, or an event. A member's post is a lead, not a fact. It might be old, about a different place, or simply wrong. Read the group's rules and keep private details out of public questions. For hours, eligibility, or what to bring, check the organization's own page or call its listed number. That is the same habit you used with AI answers in Week 2. Open the Mission 4C Practice page and practice the meeting controls. Then, list your meeting habits and one community claim you would check yourself. Pause the video now.

Here are two fictional streaming offers. Offer A is free for 30 days, then $6 a month until you cancel. Offer B is $60 a year, paid now. Free does not mean free forever. After the first month, A charges you every month, so a full year of A costs $66. Before you agree, find the seller, the price now, the price later, the renewal date, and how to cancel. Deleting the app does not cancel the subscription. Pay with a credit card, which lets you dispute a wrong charge. Person -to -person apps are for people you know. Work out both offers for 3 months and for 12, and write 2 questions to ask. Pause the video now.

Good coordination leaves a trail anyone can follow. By the end of today, Sam knows what to review and by when. Pat can see the notice without the volunteers seeing one another. Everyone works from one shared copy and every comment ends with a reply and a decision. In meetings, you test first, take turns, and ask before recording. Before you pay for anything, you know what it will cost in a year and how to stop it. Pick one habit to use this week, a clearer subject line, fewer recipients, one shared copy, or a check before you pay.

Online safety is not about being afraid of your computer. It is a set of small decisions you already know how to make. You would not hand your house key to a stranger who knocked on the door, and you would not sign a paper without reading it. The same judgment works online. Today, you will set up your station so it is comfortable, spot a scam and check it a safer way, and protect your devices and files. Then, you will show five skills from this course and take the post test. Each step starts the same way. Pause, look closely, and check before you act.

Start with your body and your screen. Sit so you can read without leaning in. The screen should be about an arm's length away with the top near eye level. If the words are too small, magnifier makes everything bigger. Press the Windows key and plus to zoom in and the Windows key and escape to close it. Browser zoom is different. It enlarges one website and control and zero puts it back. Change one thing at a time, notice what got easier, and put shared settings back before you leave. If alerts keep pulling you away, do not disturb quiets them while you work.

Some features help far more people than you might expect. Captions help in a noisy room, in a quiet library, and for anyone who hears less than they used to. Keyboard access helps someone who cannot use a mouse. Press Tab and a visible outline moves from one control to the next. Color is another one. If a schedule shows full shifts only in dark shading, some people will miss it, and so will a black and white printer. Put a word beside the color. Mute this week's video, read its captions, and press Tab to watch the outline move. Pause the video now.

Here is a fictional message. The subject says, act now. Account will close. It comes from support at account -check .example, and it asks you to verify your password immediately. Three things should slow you down. The message pushes you to hurry. The sender does not match any organization you deal with. And it asks for a password, which a real organization will not request by email. A familiar logo proves nothing because anyone can copy a logo. Spelling can be perfect and the message can still be fake. This kind of fake message is called phishing.

Never use the link or the phone number inside a suspicious message. Reach the organization another way. Open a bookmark you saved, type an address you know, or call the number on your card or letter. Then ask whether the problem is real. If you already typed your password, go to the real site, change it, and turn on two -step verification so a code is needed as well. Then tell someone who can help. Open the Mission 5B Practice page. Inspect the subject, the sender, and the link, and write two warning signs and you're safe or check. Pause the video now.

Not every risk arrives as an email. A new online friend may be warm and patient for weeks, then ask for money, often gift cards, and ask you to keep it secret. Secrecy and money together are a reason to stop and check with someone you trust. Scrolling late at night because you might miss something is a real pull too. Set a stopping point or quiet your alerts. If someone posts something hurtful about you, do not reply in anger. Keep a screenshot if it is safe, report or block, and talk to someone. Write a safe next step for each situation on your worksheet. Pause the video now.

Updates fix security holes, so let Windows Update do its job. Home computers still on Windows 10 need extended security updates, which run through October 2027, or a move to a supported device. A website may ask to use your camera or microphone. Allow it when the task needs it, such as a video meeting, and block it when it does not, such as a page you only read. A permission can stay on after a call ends, so check it in your browser settings now and then. If you find a USB drive you do not recognize, do not plug it in. Give it to staff.

Different protections do different jobs. In Word, a password to open a file encrypts it so nobody can read it without that password. Read -only only limits changes. Anyone can still read the words. Device encryption protects a laptop that is lost while turned off. None of these protect a computer left signed in, so press Windows and L to lock it or sign out of a shared computer. For accounts, use a pass key when a site offers one. Otherwise, use a long, unique passphrase with two -step verification. On the Mission 5C Practice page, choose before you flip each card, then look at the settings your worksheet names. Pause the video now.

But now you get to show what you can do. The Skills Challenge has five tasks, and you work on your own. Ask a search question that names the place and open the organization's own page. Build a short word paragraph with a real heading, three numbered steps, and a bold warning. Total four costs in Excel with a formula. Delete a line, then bring it back with Undo. and write useful feedback on a partner's flyer. The quick card is allowed. Your instructor watches and records how much help you needed. This is separate from your test score, and it shows what you can already do on your own.

Last comes the post test. It has 20 questions and you take it on your own with no coaching. When you finish, submit your results to Brit and save the complete graded PDF. The results show your score and which areas went well. Treat them as a learning plan, not a verdict. Pick one strength to keep using and one skill to practice next. Then, compare where you started on the pretest with where you are now. Every row you completed in this course is something you can do again, at home, at your own pace.

An AI coding agent is a program that reads the files of an app, plans a change, edits the code, and can run checks, all from a request written in plain English. That sounds like magic, but it is closer to hiring a fast helper who has never met you. It does exactly what it understood, which is not always what you meant. Today you will direct one. Our app is a small fictional community resource finder. You will ask for one change, read what the agent changed, test it, and report a problem. Then we look at what it would take to turn this page into a real service.

Before you ask for any change, find out what works now. Open version 1 of the Resource Finder and try a few searches. Library finds one resource. Library in capital letters also finds one, because the page ignores capital letters. But learning finds nothing, even though two resources are about learning. Version 1 only searches names and descriptions, not categories. That is the one thing we want changed. Writing down what works today also tells you what must not break tomorrow. Search version 1 for library, library, learning, community, and zzzz. And write down each result. Pause the video now.

A spec is a careful request. It names one change, who it helps, and what must stay the same. Hours says, let the search also find resources by category for visitors who know the kind of help, but not the name. Keep capital letters matching and keep the message that appears when nothing matches. Then add acceptance checks, tests anyone can run. I type learning. I expect two resources. I type library. I expect one. Never put real names, passwords, or secret keys in a request. Write your spec and three checks a partner could run. Pause the video now.

A good agent can show its plan before it touches anything. Ask for that. Some agents can also work on their own for a while, and you choose how much freedom to give. Either way, you review every change before you accept it. Read the plan and make a prediction. Which part of the page will change? About how many lines? What could break? Predicting first makes you a sharper reviewer because you know what to look for. Write your prediction, the part that will change, about how many lines, and one thing that could break. Pause the video now.

a diff shows exactly what changed. A line with a minus sign was removed, and a line with a plus sign was added. Here, one added line puts the category into the search. That is what we asked for. But look closer. Another line lost three words written together in the code. Two lowercase. That is the step that ignores capital letters. Nobody asked for that. You can check it yourself. Press CTRL and U to see the page's code, then CTRL and F to search it for 2 lowercase. Version 1 has 2 matches, and version 2 has 1. Open the Mission 6B Practice page page, and mark each changed line as asked for or not. Pause the video now.

Now test the agents version, called version 2. Start with the happy path, the normal use you expect to work. Type learning and two resources appear. Type library and one appears. Type ZZZ and the no match message shows. Then try capital letters. Type library and nothing is found. Version 1 found it. Something that used to work and broke after a change is called a regression. Keep going, because one failure does not end a test. Check that tab moves a clear outline through the controls, and that the page still works in a narrow window. Run the five checks in your test log. Pause the video now.

A bug report is a request a stranger could follow. Give the steps. Open version 2 and type library. Give what you expected. One resource as version 1 found. Give what actually happened. No matches. Then say what must stay the same. Keep the new category search. That last part matters because a careless fix can undo the work you wanted. Saying it is broken gives the agent nothing to act on. A clear report usually gets a small, careful repair. Write a repair request with the steps, what you expected, what happened, and what to keep. Pause the video now.

The agent sends back version 3. Do not trust it until you retest. First, repeat the check that failed. Type library, and one resource appears again. Then repeat checks that passed before, because fixing one thing can break another. Learning still finds 2, and zzzz still shows the no match message. Only when the failed check passes and nothing else broke do you accept the repair. repair. This loop is the whole job. Ask clearly, read the change, test it, report it, and retest. Run your checks on version 3 and decide whether to accept the repair. Pause the video now.

Our finder is one page with fictional data. A real service needs much more. It needs an address, a domain name you rent every year. It needs a home. Hosting is a computer that keeps the site running so anyone with the address can use it. To save favorites for many people, it needs a back end, the part on a server that stores data. Sign -in must be checked on that server, never by a picture of a sign -in box. A secret API key, the code that lets your app use a paid service, stays on the server too. Plan the Finder as a real service, one roadblock at a time. Pause the video now.
